newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia expects speedy return to IMF.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia expects speedy return to IMF.

text.p: Yugoslavia expects to get access to international financial markets in the near future, a senior government official said on Friday.
"I believe the moment is approaching when Yugoslavia will normalise relations with international financial institutions," federal Finance Minister Tomica Raicevic said.
The Yugoslav parliament on Thursday endorsed the federal government's plan for a speedy return to and normalisation of relations with the IMF and other financial organisations.
"All the relevant conditions set by the IMF in its decision of December 14, 1992 have been met," Raicevic said in his statement faxed to Reuters.
"All conditions now exist for Yugoslavia to normalise relations with the Fund and other financial institutions," he said.
But the statement did not spell out whether Yugoslavia gave up its demand to be the only legal successor to former Yugoslav federation - the core of a longtime dispute with the IMF.

After the parliament session on Thursday Raicevic explicitly said Yugoslavia has accepted the IMF quota of 36.52 percent in dividing assets and liabilities of former Yugoslavia -- but only in the case of the fund.
"We do not renounce our stands regarding international legal personality and continuity," he said.
The government also accepted to pay back its outstanding debt of $104 million.

Earlier this month the government also adopted a decree on the country's membership with the IMF based on the December 14, 1992 decision of the IMF Board of Directors which was endorsed by the parliament on Thursday.
"The decree is very important for Yugoslav return to the international financial community," Raicevic said in its written statement.
"It was adopted with the consent of the Fund in constructive efforts to find a solution which would satisfy the interests of both sides," he said.

Yugoslavia's membership in the IMF has been a cause of major dispute among politicians in Serbia. Hardliners have demanded Belgrade be given the rights of the old Yugoslav federation as its successor state, while moderates have urged a prudent and pragmatic approach.
The dispute led to the ousting in May of popular National Bank governor Dragoslav Avramovic who championed the latter.
But facing an economic disaster at home without fresh foreign capital, the Yugoslav government appears to have backed down and accepted the IMF's conditions for membership.
Raicevic said that Yugoslavia was also making efforts to normalise its relations with its other creditors, above all, with commercial banks.
